title: Local Storage Options on Mobile
summary: Preferences, embedded databases, files, and secure storage each solve a different data shape. Learn the decision framework before you reach for Room or Core Data specifics.

slides.markdown:
Every mobile app eventually needs to remember something after it closes — a setting, a login token, a cached feed, a downloaded file. The mistake beginners make is reaching for one storage mechanism and forcing everything through it: an object graph serialized into preferences, or a photo stuffed into a database column.

Mobile platforms give you four distinct storage tiers, each shaped for a different kind of data: **preferences, an embedded database, raw files, and secure storage**. Picking the right tier is a five-minute decision that saves weeks of migration pain later. This topic is the decision framework; Room and Core Data's concrete APIs belong to Android and iOS.

| Tier | Shape it fits | Typical size | Query needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Preferences** | Flat key-value settings | A few KB | Read one key by name |
| **Database** | Structured, related records | MBs to GBs | Filter, join, sort |
| **Files** | Blobs — images, downloads, exports | KBs to GBs | Whole-object read/write |
| **Secure storage** | Secrets — tokens, credentials | Tiny | Read one key, hardware-backed |

The axis that actually matters is **shape and query need**, not size alone. A single JSON blob and a relational dataset can be the same number of bytes but belong in different tiers, because one needs "read this one thing" and the other needs "find all rows where...".

slides.sectionTitle: What belongs in key-value prefs vs a real database
slides.markdown:
Preferences APIs (`SharedPreferences`/`DataStore` on Android, `UserDefaults` on iOS) are a flat map of primitives to primitives. They're fast, simple, and tempting — which is exactly how they get abused.

**Fits prefs**: a theme choice, a feature-flag override, "has the user seen this onboarding tooltip," a last-sync timestamp — small, independent, no relationships between them.

**Does not fit prefs**: a list of orders, a user's saved addresses, anything with a one-to-many relationship, anything you'll ever need to query ("give me all unread messages"). Some teams serialize a whole object list to JSON and stuff it in one preference key — this works until the list grows, at which point every read and write touches the entire blob, and there's no way to update one item without rewriting all of them.

The test: if you'll ever ask a "which ones..." question about the data, it's a database problem, not a preferences problem.

slides.sectionTitle: Embedded SQL databases on device: why SQLite won
slides.markdown:
Both major platforms ship the same embedded database under the hood: **SQLite**. It's a serverless, single-file, zero-configuration relational engine — no daemon to start, no network port, no separate process — which is exactly what a sandboxed mobile app needs.

It won for reasons that map directly onto mobile constraints: the whole engine is a small linkable library (no install step), a database is one file you can back up or wipe with the filesystem, it's transactional and crash-safe (a kill mid-write doesn't corrupt it), and it's been battle-tested across billions of devices for two decades.

On Android, Room sits on top of raw SQLite as a type-safe query layer. On iOS, Core Data and the newer SwiftData both use SQLite as a default backing store. You're almost never talking to SQLite's C API directly — you're using it through an ORM — but understanding it's SQLite underneath explains why migrations, indexes, and query plans behave the way they do.

slides.sectionTitle: When a document store beats relational on-device
slides.markdown:
Relational is the right default, but a document/NoSQL store (Realm, an embedded key-object store) earns its place when your data is genuinely **schema-flexible or deeply nested**.

Good fit: a cache of heterogeneous API responses where each object type has different fields and you don't want a migration every time the backend adds one; an offline-first app syncing arbitrary JSON documents; data with deep object graphs (an order containing line items containing options) where a relational join would be expensive relative to just reading the whole nested object.

Poor fit: data you'll frequently query across records by field ("all orders over $50"), or where strict consistency between related tables matters — relational engines and their transaction guarantees are built for exactly that. Most apps are best served by relational for their core domain data and reach for a document store only for a specific cache or sync layer, not as a wholesale replacement.

slides.sectionTitle: Choosing a storage layer by data shape and size
slides.markdown:
The decision collapses to three questions asked in order: **Is it a secret? Is it structured/queryable? Is it a large blob?**

- Secret (token, credential) → secure storage, regardless of size.
- Structured and queryable (records, relationships) → database.
- Large binary blob (image, video, downloaded file) → filesystem, with just a path or ID reference stored in the database.
- Small, flat, independent → preferences.

The most common real-world shape is actually a **combination**: a database row holding metadata (filename, size, upload date) plus a file on disk holding the actual bytes, linked by a path. Storing a large blob directly in a database column works technically but bloats query performance and backup size for no benefit.

slides.sectionTitle: Encrypting data at rest: what the OS gives you for free
slides.markdown:
Modern mobile OSes encrypt the entire device storage at rest by default, tied to the device passcode/biometric — this is **full-disk encryption**, and it happens whether your app does anything or not.

But full-disk encryption protects against one threat model: someone physically pulling the device's storage chip. It does **not** protect data from another app on a rooted/jailbroken device, from a backup that gets extracted, or from the data being readable the instant the device is unlocked (which is most of the time it's in someone's pocket).

For genuinely sensitive data, the platforms layer additional guarantees on top: file-level encryption classes that stay locked until after first unlock, and hardware-backed secure storage (below) for the highest-sensitivity items. The practical rule: full-disk encryption is the floor, not the ceiling — treat it as covering "lost or stolen device, powered off," and use secure storage for anything that needs more.

slides.sectionTitle: Secure storage for tokens and secrets
slides.markdown:
Auth tokens, refresh tokens, and API keys need a tier above regular files: **hardware-backed secure storage** — the Keystore on Android, the Keychain on iOS. Both are backed by a dedicated secure element or trusted execution environment separate from main app storage.

What that buys you: the OS (not your app) manages the encryption keys, keys can be marked non-exportable so even a compromised OS can't extract the raw key material, and access can be gated behind biometric or passcode re-authentication for especially sensitive operations.

What it doesn't buy you: protection if the app itself is compromised and simply asks the Keychain/Keystore for the decrypted secret through the legitimate API — secure storage protects the *storage*, not a malicious or vulnerable client. It's necessary but not sufficient; you still need to think about who inside your own app can read the token once it's decrypted in memory.

slides.sectionTitle: Migrating an on-device schema without losing user data
slides.markdown:
Unlike a server database with one schema version live at a time, an on-device app has **every version you ever shipped, still installed on real devices**, all needing a path forward. A user can skip three app versions between opens and their local database has to migrate through all of them.

The safe pattern: versioned, additive migrations that run in order (v3→v4→v5, never v3→v5 directly, so each step stays simple and testable) and never destructively drop a column or table unless you've confirmed no live version needs it. Both Room and Core Data support declaring a schema version and writing an explicit migration for each step; skipping a version or mismatching the declared version is the single most common cause of "app crashes on update for some users."

Always test migrating from your **oldest still-supported version**, not just the previous one — that's the path real long-time users will actually take, and it's the one nobody manually tests by default.

slides.sectionTitle: Sensitive data in plain preferences, and unbounded local caches
slides.markdown:
Two mistakes that ship constantly:

**Storing a token in plain preferences.** `SharedPreferences`/`UserDefaults` are convenient and *feel* private because they're sandboxed to your app, but they are not encrypted at the app layer and are readable on a rooted/jailbroken device or in a full backup extraction. A leaked auth token from a preferences file is a real, recurring class of mobile vulnerability report.

**An unbounded local cache.** A feed or image cache that only ever grows — no eviction, no size cap — will eventually fill the device's disk, and the first symptom users report is unrelated: "my phone says storage full" or a *different* app failing to save a photo. The fix is a bounded cache with an eviction policy (LRU by size or age) checked in, not something added after a support escalation.

Both mistakes share a root cause: treating device storage as free and infinite because it's not billed per-byte the way server storage is.
